items.stem: Which of the following best describes "line of symmetry"?
options: The fixed point that does not move during a rotation
A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks the same after a rotation of less than 360° about its centre
The number by which every length is multiplied in an enlargement
A line that divides a shape into two halves that are mirror images of each other
items.answer: A line that divides a shape into two halves that are mirror images of each other
items.markingKey: D. "line of symmetry" is a line that divides a shape into two halves that are mirror images of each other.

items.stem: "A rectangle has 4 lines of symmetry because it has 4 sides." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Only the two lines through the midpoints of opposite sides work; the diagonals are not lines of symmetry.
items.markingKey: Only the two lines through the midpoints of opposite sides work; the diagonals are not lines of symmetry. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why every shape has rotational symmetry of at least order 1.
items.answer: Every shape looks the same after a full 360° turn, so the count is at least 1; "no rotational symmetry" means order 1. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Every shape looks the same after a full 360° turn, so the count is at least 1; "no rotational symmetry" means order 1. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A regular polygon has 7 sides. State its number of lines of symmetry, its order of rotational symmetry, and the smallest angle of rotation that maps it onto itself.
items.answer: 7 lines; order 7; 51.43°

items.stem: Alessia shades 1 of the 3 identical sectors of a circle cut into 3 equal sectors, all next to each other. State the order of rotational symmetry and the number of lines of symmetry of the pattern.
items.answer: order 1; 1 line
items.markingKey: Shaded block of adjacent sectors only repeats after a full turn (R1): order 1 (A1); one line through the middle of the block (A1).

items.stem: A car-parts firm in Oslo designs a wheel hubcap with 12 identical, evenly spaced spokes, each symmetric about its own centre line. (a) Find the angle between neighbouring spokes. (b) State the order of rotational symmetry and the number of lines of symmetry. (c) The spokes are then painted alternately red and silver. Find the new order and number of lines, and explain the change.
items.answer: (a) 30° (b) order 12, 12 lines (c) order 6, 6 lines; the colours only repeat every 60°
items.markingKey: (a) 30° (b) order 12, 12 lines (c) order 6, 6 lines; the colours only repeat every 60°. Symmetry correctly identified (A1 A1); pattern or design justified (B: R1); angles stated with correct notation (C1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The number of times a shape looks the same during one full turn"?
items.answer: order of rotational symmetry
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of order of rotational symmetry.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "order of rotational symmetry".
items.answer: The number of times a shape looks the same during one full turn
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the number of times a shape looks the same during one full turn. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Zara says a regular 10-sided polygon has rotational symmetry of order 10 because it fits onto itself every 36°. Explain why this reasoning is correct.
items.answer: All sides and angles are equal, so turning through 360° ÷ 10 = 36° takes each vertex to the next; this happens 10 times in a full turn.
items.markingKey: Equal sides/angles (R1); angle 360/n and count (R1).

items.stem: Briefly explain why a parallelogram has no lines of symmetry even though it has rotational symmetry.
items.answer: Folding along a diagonal or a midline does not make the halves match, but a half-turn about the centre maps it onto itself.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Folding along a diagonal or a midline does not make the halves match, but a half-turn about the centre maps it onto itself. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Alessia shades 3 of the 4 identical sectors of a circle cut into 4 equal sectors, all next to each other. State the order of rotational symmetry and the number of lines of symmetry of the pattern.
items.answer: order 1; 1 line
items.markingKey: Shaded block of adjacent sectors only repeats after a full turn (R1): order 1 (A1); one line through the middle of the block (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "A shape with no rotational symmetry has order 0." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The order is at least 1, because every shape fits onto itself after a full turn.
items.markingKey: The order is at least 1, because every shape fits onto itself after a full turn. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: State the number of lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of a isosceles triangle (not equilateral).
items.answer: 1 line; order 1
items.markingKey: Lines: 1 (A1); order 1 (A1).

items.stem: Sofia investigates the symmetry of regular polygons. (a) Complete a table for the equilateral triangle, square, regular pentagon and regular hexagon showing the number of lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry. (b) Describe the pattern in words. (c) Predict the symmetry of a regular 14-gon and the smallest angle of rotation that maps it onto itself.
items.answer: (a) 3, 3; 4, 4; 5, 5; 6, 6 (b) a regular n-gon has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n (c) 14 lines, order 14, smallest angle 25.71°
items.markingKey: (a) 3, 3; 4, 4; 5, 5; 6, 6 (b) a regular n-gon has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n (c) 14 lines, order 14, smallest angle 25.71°. Symmetry correctly identified (A1 A1); pattern or design justified (B: R1); angles stated with correct notation (C1).

items.stem: A festival banner in Accra shows a regular star with 5 points. (a) State the number of lines of symmetry. (b) State the order of rotational symmetry. (c) Find the angle at the centre between two neighbouring points. (d) Does the star have the same symmetry as a regular 5-sided polygon? Justify your answer.
items.answer: (a) 5 lines (b) order 5 (c) 72° (d) yes – each point maps onto the next after 72°, the same as for a regular 5-gon
items.markingKey: (a) 5 lines (b) order 5 (c) 72° (d) yes – each point maps onto the next after 72°, the same as for a regular 5-gon. Symmetry correctly identified (A1 A1); pattern or design justified (B: R1); angles stated with correct notation (C1).

items.stem: What is the image of (2, 5) after reflection in the line y = x?
items.markingKey: (5, 2). Reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a translated shape is congruent to the original shape.
items.answer: Every point moves by the same vector, so all lengths and angles stay the same; only the position changes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Every point moves by the same vector, so all lengths and angles stay the same; only the position changes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The point (1, 5) maps to (5, 1). Explain which single reflection does this.
items.answer: Reflection in the line y = x, which swaps the x- and y-coordinates.
items.markingKey: Coordinates swapped (R1); line y = x (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "Reflecting (5, 1) in the y-axis gives (5, −1)." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Reflection in the y-axis changes the sign of x: (−5, 1).
items.markingKey: Reflection in the y-axis changes the sign of x: (−5, 1). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Triangle ABC has vertices A(0, 0), B(4, −2) and C(3, −6). It is translated by (−6 over 2). Find the vertices of the image A′B′C′.
items.markingKey: Vector added to each vertex (M1); all three correct (A1 A1).

items.stem: Triangle T has vertices (1, 1), (4, 1) and (1, 3). (a) Reflect T in the y-axis to give T₁. (b) Reflect T₁ in the x-axis to give T₂. (c) Describe fully a single transformation that maps T to T₂.
items.markingKey: (a) (−1, 1), (−4, 1), (−1, 3) (b) (−1, −1), (−4, −1), (−1, −3) (c) rotation of 180° about the origin. Each transformation applied (M1 A1 A1); combined transformation described fully with correct vocabulary (C1 R1).

items.stem: Define the term "image".
items.answer: The shape (or point) produced by a transformation; the original is the object
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the shape (or point) produced by a transformation; the original is the object. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a reflection changes the orientation of a shape but a translation does not.
items.answer: A reflection flips the shape over, so the order of vertices (clockwise/anticlockwise) is reversed; a translation only slides it.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A reflection flips the shape over, so the order of vertices (clockwise/anticlockwise) is reversed; a translation only slides it. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The column vector (3 over −2) means 3 up and 2 left." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The top number is horizontal: 3 right; the bottom number is vertical: 2 down.
items.markingKey: The top number is horizontal: 3 right; the bottom number is vertical: 2 down. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A point P(6, −4) is reflected to P′(−6, −4). Find the equation of the mirror line and explain how you know.
items.markingKey: The mirror line is halfway between P and P′ and perpendicular to PP′ (R1): midpoint x = (6 + −6)/2 = 0 (A1).

items.stem: Find the image of (−3, 0) after reflection in the line y = −x.
items.markingKey: Rule for reflection in the line y = −x applied (M1); (0, 3) (A1).

items.stem: Reflect the point (−6, 3) in the line x = −2. Give the coordinates of the image and explain your method.
items.markingKey: Distance from the point to the line is the same on the other side (M1); (2, 3) (A1); method explained (C1).

items.stem: A point moves from (1, 0) to (3, 1). Write down the column vector of the translation, and describe it in words.
items.answer: (2 over 1): 2 right, 1 up
items.markingKey: Image − object: (3 − 1, 1 − 0) (M1); vector (A1); description (C1).

items.stem: Investigate reflecting the point (4, 2) in the line x = 1 and then in the line x = 0. (a) Find both images. (b) Describe the single transformation from the original point to the final image. (c) Predict what happens for any two parallel mirror lines a distance k apart.
items.answer: (a) (−2, 2), then (2, 2) (b) a translation by (−2 over 0) (c) two reflections in parallel lines k apart give a translation of 2k perpendicular to the lines
items.markingKey: (a) (−2, 2), then (2, 2) (b) a translation by (−2 over 0) (c) two reflections in parallel lines k apart give a translation of 2k perpendicular to the lines. Each transformation applied (M1 A1 A1); combined transformation described fully with correct vocabulary (C1 R1).

items.stem: A robot on a warehouse grid starts at (1, 1). It is moved by the translation (−3 over −4) and then by (4 over 1). (a) Find its final position. (b) Write a single column vector for the combined move. (c) Explain why the order of the two translations does not matter.
items.answer: (a) (2, −2) (b) (1 over −3) (c) vector addition is commutative: (−3 + 4, −4 + 1) is the same either way
items.markingKey: (a) (2, −2) (b) (1 over −3) (c) vector addition is commutative: (−3 + 4, −4 + 1) is the same either way. Each transformation applied (M1 A1 A1); combined transformation described fully with correct vocabulary (C1 R1).

items.markingKey: D. 90° anticlockwise: (7, 3) → (−3, 7).

items.stem: "A rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin maps (2, 5) to (−2, 5)." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: 90° clockwise maps (x, y) to (y, −x), so the image is (5, −2).
items.markingKey: 90° clockwise maps (x, y) to (y, −x), so the image is (5, −2). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why you must state the angle, the direction and the centre to describe a rotation fully.
items.answer: The same angle about a different centre, or in the other direction, gives a different image; all three are needed to define it uniquely.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The same angle about a different centre, or in the other direction, gives a different image; all three are needed to define it uniquely. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: (4, −1), (2, −4), (6, −2); fourth quadrant

items.stem: Investigate rotating the point A(1, 6) repeatedly by 90° clockwise about the origin. (a) Find the images A₁, A₂, A₃ and A₄. (b) Describe the shape formed by A, A₁, A₂, A₃. (c) Explain why A₄ = A.
items.answer: (a) (6, −1), (−1, −6), (−6, 1), (1, 6) (b) a square centred on the origin (c) four quarter turns make a full turn of 360°
items.markingKey: (a) (6, −1), (−1, −6), (−6, 1), (1, 6) (b) a square centred on the origin (c) four quarter turns make a full turn of 360°. Rotation rules applied (M1 A1 A1); pattern / symmetry identified (B: R1); clear notation (C1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The same shape but possibly a different size; corresponding angles equal and sides in the same ratio"?

items.stem: Explain how to find the centre of an enlargement from a shape and its image.

items.stem: A design student in Nairobi wants a pinwheel logo with rotational symmetry of order 4 but no lines of symmetry. (a) Describe how many identical arms are needed and how they are placed. (b) Explain why the logo has no lines of symmetry. (c) List every angle of rotation between 0° and 360° (inclusive) that maps the logo onto itself.
items.answer: (a) 4 identical arms, each turned 90° from the last (b) 0 lines – the arms are bent the same way, so no fold matches them (c) 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°
items.markingKey: (a) 4 identical arms, each turned 90° from the last (b) 0 lines – the arms are bent the same way, so no fold matches them (c) 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. Symmetry correctly identified (A1 A1); pattern or design justified (B: R1); angles stated with correct notation (C1).

items.stem: A robot on a warehouse grid starts at (−2, 4). It is moved by the translation (−3 over 3) and then by (−4 over −4). (a) Find its final position. (b) Write a single column vector for the combined move. (c) Explain why the order of the two translations does not matter.
items.answer: (a) (−9, 3) (b) (−7 over −1) (c) vector addition is commutative: (−3 + −4, 3 + −4) is the same either way
items.markingKey: (a) (−9, 3) (b) (−7 over −1) (c) vector addition is commutative: (−3 + −4, 3 + −4) is the same either way. Each transformation applied (M1 A1 A1); combined transformation described fully with correct vocabulary (C1 R1).

items.stem: The point P(3, 4) is rotated 180° about C(1, 2) and then 90° clockwise about the same centre. (a) Find the image after the first rotation. (b) Find the final image. (c) Describe fully the single rotation that has the same effect, and check it using P.
items.answer: (a) (−1, 0) (b) (−1, 4) (c) a rotation of 90° anticlockwise (270° clockwise) about (1, 2); check: (3, 4) → (−1, 4)
items.markingKey: (a) (−1, 0) (b) (−1, 4) (c) a rotation of 90° anticlockwise (270° clockwise) about (1, 2); check: (3, 4) → (−1, 4). Rotation rules applied (M1 A1 A1); pattern / symmetry identified (B: R1); clear notation (C1).

items.stem: A poster design is 9 cm by 6 cm. It is enlarged by scale factor 3 for a bus shelter in Geneva. (a) Find the dimensions of the enlarged poster. (b) How many times more ink is needed (assuming ink is proportional to area)? (c) The printer offers scale factor 4 for the same price. Explain the effect on the area.
items.answer: (a) 27 cm by 18 cm (b) 9 times (c) the area would be 16 × 54 = 864 cm², 16 times the original
items.markingKey: (a) 27 cm by 18 cm (b) 9 times (c) the area would be 16 × 54 = 864 cm², 16 times the original. Length scale factor applied (M1 A1); area factor k² (M1 A1); reasoning communicated (R1).

items.stem: Which letter has rotational symmetry of order 2 but no line of symmetry?
items.answer: S
items.markingKey: C. S looks the same after a half turn but cannot be folded onto itself.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A vector (a over b) that describes a translation: a units right (left if negative) and b units up (down if negative)"?
items.answer: column vector
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of column vector.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "clockwise".
items.answer: Turning in the same direction as the hands of a clock
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: turning in the same direction as the hands of a clock. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "An enlargement with scale factor 1/3 makes the shape bigger." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A scale factor between 0 and 1 makes the image smaller (one third of the lengths).
items.markingKey: A scale factor between 0 and 1 makes the image smaller (one third of the lengths). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the link between the number of sides of a regular polygon and its symmetry.
items.answer: A regular n-gon has n equal sides and angles, so it has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n (it matches every 360°/n).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A regular n-gon has n equal sides and angles, so it has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n (it matches every 360°/n). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The point (6, 0) maps to (0, 6). Explain which single reflection does this.
items.answer: Reflection in the line y = x, which swaps the x- and y-coordinates.
items.markingKey: Coordinates swapped (R1); line y = x (A1).

items.stem: Explain why a rotation of 180° does not need a direction.
items.answer: Turning half a turn clockwise or anticlockwise ends in the same place.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Turning half a turn clockwise or anticlockwise ends in the same place. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why two triangles with sides 4, 6, 7 cm and 8, 12, 14 cm are similar but not congruent.
items.answer: Corresponding sides are all in the ratio 1 : 2, so one is an enlargement of the other (similar); the sides are not equal, so they are not congruent.
items.markingKey: Common ratio (R1); congruent needs equal sides (R1).

items.stem: Chloé says a regular 7-sided polygon has rotational symmetry of order 7 because it fits onto itself every 51.43°. Explain why this reasoning is correct.
items.answer: All sides and angles are equal, so turning through 360° ÷ 7 = 51.43° takes each vertex to the next; this happens 7 times in a full turn.
items.markingKey: Equal sides/angles (R1); angle 360/n and count (R1).

items.stem: Triangle ABC has vertices A(1, 0), B(0, 4) and C(5, 5). It is translated by (0 over −3). Find the vertices of the image A′B′C′.
items.markingKey: Vector added to each vertex (M1); all three correct (A1 A1).

items.stem: Triangle PQR has vertices P(1, 4), Q(4, 4) and R(4, 5). It is rotated 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Find the image vertices and state the quadrant the image lies in.
items.answer: (−4, 1), (−4, 4), (−5, 4); second quadrant
items.markingKey: Rotation rule applied to each vertex (M1 A1 A1); quadrant (A1).

items.stem: A photo 24 cm wide is enlarged to 96 cm wide. Find the scale factor and the new height if the original height was 14 cm.
items.answer: scale factor 4; height 56 cm

items.stem: Mateo shades 4 of the 5 identical sectors of a circle cut into 5 equal sectors, all next to each other. State the order of rotational symmetry and the number of lines of symmetry of the pattern.
items.answer: order 1; 1 line
items.markingKey: Shaded block of adjacent sectors only repeats after a full turn (R1): order 1 (A1); one line through the middle of the block (A1).

items.stem: Find the image of (4, 2) after reflection in the line y = x.
items.markingKey: Rule for reflection in the line y = x applied (M1); (2, 4) (A1).

items.stem: Rotate the point (1, −2) through 90° anticlockwise about the centre (3, 2). Find its image.
items.markingKey: Position relative to the centre (−2, −4) (M1); rotated (4, −2) (A1); add back the centre: (7, 0) (A1).

items.stem: Triangle ABC has vertices (5, 3), (6, −5), (0, −3). Enlarge it by scale factor 4 with centre (3, −1). Find the coordinates of the image.
items.markingKey: Vector from the centre to each vertex multiplied by 4 (M1); all three images (A1 A1).

items.stem: A design student in Cape Town wants a pinwheel logo with rotational symmetry of order 3 but no lines of symmetry. (a) Describe how many identical arms are needed and how they are placed. (b) Explain why the logo has no lines of symmetry. (c) List every angle of rotation between 0° and 360° (inclusive) that maps the logo onto itself.
items.answer: (a) 3 identical arms, each turned 120° from the last (b) 0 lines – the arms are bent the same way, so no fold matches them (c) 120°, 240°, 360°

items.stem: A robot on a warehouse grid starts at (3, −1). It is moved by the translation (5 over −5) and then by (5 over −4). (a) Find its final position. (b) Write a single column vector for the combined move. (c) Explain why the order of the two translations does not matter.
items.answer: (a) (13, −10) (b) (10 over −9) (c) vector addition is commutative: (5 + 5, −5 + −4) is the same either way
items.markingKey: (a) (13, −10) (b) (10 over −9) (c) vector addition is commutative: (5 + 5, −5 + −4) is the same either way. Each transformation applied (M1 A1 A1); combined transformation described fully with correct vocabulary (C1 R1).

items.stem: The point P(6, 3) is rotated 180° about C(3, 2) and then 90° clockwise about the same centre. (a) Find the image after the first rotation. (b) Find the final image. (c) Describe fully the single rotation that has the same effect, and check it using P.
items.answer: (a) (0, 1) (b) (2, 5) (c) a rotation of 90° anticlockwise (270° clockwise) about (3, 2); check: (6, 3) → (2, 5)
items.markingKey: (a) (0, 1) (b) (2, 5) (c) a rotation of 90° anticlockwise (270° clockwise) about (3, 2); check: (6, 3) → (2, 5). Rotation rules applied (M1 A1 A1); pattern / symmetry identified (B: R1); clear notation (C1).

(b) How many times more ink is needed (assuming ink is proportional to area)? (c) The printer offers scale factor 6 for the same price. Explain the effect on the area.
items.answer: (a) 35 cm by 25 cm (b) 25 times (c) the area would be 36 × 35 = 1260 cm², 36 times the original
